<reason>Both sides argued well and narrowed cleanly. A (CON) ran a disciplined epistemic case — underpowered nulls, no pre-registered equivalence testing, best-case Northern European registries, and a genuinely clever selection dilemma turning B's own mechanism. But A's route never escaped two decisive counters. First, B's parity-of-standards point (no family form — stepfamilies, single fathers, adoptive families — has passed the equivalence test A demands, so A's standard is a veto on evidence rather than rigor) was never squarely answered. Second, B turned A's own stepfamily example [A2.4] into a sensitivity proof: the same research tradition reliably detects divorce and stepfamily gaps yet registers nothing for parental gender, which materially blunts the power objection. Third, and most importantly, the motion asks whether children "do as well on average," and A's final characterisation — "a rough wash between conceded advantages and conceded disadvantages" — concedes equal average outcomes while disputing only the epistemic label; B's "parity is my claim" landed on this and A never dislodged it. A's late-named mechanism (biological separation) was legitimately introduced under pressure, but B dissolved it efficiently: it is shared by adoptive and donor-conceived children of different-sex couples, is not gender-caused, and those children are inside the registry data. On the policy limb, A's concession of custody/benefits/hospital access left B's second limb largely intact; A's clarified opposition (courts taking judicial notice) was a real distinction but thin next to B's framing of codified suspicion. A also paid an execution cost with a clipped, over-length opening that truncated its policy argument. Close and competitive, but B made the choice easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 answer [B4.1], which flipped A's stepfamily analogy: the same research tradition that detects moderate stepfamily and divorce effects registers nothing for parental gender, so the instruments are demonstrably sensitive — combined with the point that no family form has ever met A's pre-registered equivalence standard. That pair converted A's strongest methodological attack into evidence for parity and left A relying on unmeasured, unobserved harm.</best_rebuttal>
